title: "Filing a Biological Product Deviation Report"

## The form that's still blank

The plasma-labeling event is a week old. Your Quality Analyst (QA) walked you through it in
`warning-letters-and-recalls`: a reference-table error inside Fairview's BECS (Blood
Establishment Computer Software) printed one production lot's plasma containers with the
wrong subtype — standard Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) labeled as "Plasma Frozen Within 24 Hours
After Phlebotomy" (PF24), a different subtype with meaningfully different clotting-factor
levels. The lot left Fairview's control and reached one hospital transfusion service before
anyone caught it. No unit has been transfused. Your QA has already walked the six-factor
health-hazard test and reached a reasoned recommendation of Class II, and that recall
paperwork is already moving toward FDA (Food and Drug Administration).

She's back in your office with a second, separate question. "We also need to file a BPDR
(Biological Product Deviation Report) on this. I know it's reportable — that part's not in
question. What I don't actually know is how we file it, who signs it, or where it goes."

She's right that reportability isn't the open question here. A deviation that affects a
distributed blood component's identity and labeling clears that bar without a close call.
What's still sitting undone is the filing itself — the actual form, the actual office, the
actual window — and that's today's job.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Deciding something is reportable and actually reporting it are two different acts, and a
regulator who only checks the first one is checking the easy half. An organization can have
a perfect internal reportability determination — timestamped, reasoned, signed — and still
never get that information to the one federal office whose entire job is tracking patterns
across every blood establishment in the country. CBER can't act on a determination it never
receives. The filing mechanics exist because the paperwork isn't a formality on top of the
decision; it's the only part of this that actually reaches anyone outside Lakeshore.

You already run something structurally identical, and you've probably run it personally. A
security incident that crosses a reporting threshold — a data breach notification law, a
contractual SLA (service level agreement) breach notice — doesn't end when your team finishes
remediation. It triggers a separate, timed, addressed filing: a specific form or format, sent
to a specific recipient, inside a specific clock, independent of how well the remediation
itself went. Doing excellent incident response doesn't substitute for actually making that
filing, on time, to the right party, in the right format. A BPDR is that same shape, applied
to a blood component instead of a data record.

Here's where the regulated world asks for more precision than most of your compliance
filings do. An ordinary breach notice's recipient and format are often negotiable in
practice — email a named contact, use whatever template the contract specifies, adjust the
channel if the primary one is unavailable. A BPDR's recipient and acceptable formats are
fixed by regulation, not left to firm discretion: it goes to CBER specifically, not any other
FDA office, and only in one of two forms the regulation itself names. There's no "close
enough" recipient and no improvised third format.

## The rule in plain English

Three questions, in order: who reports, how, and where — plus how this duty sits next to
Lakeshore's recall and its own internal investigation.

**Who reports isn't an individual — it's the establishment, through Quality.** The
regulation's own language is "you," meaning whichever licensed manufacturer, unlicensed
registered blood establishment, or transfusion service had control over the product when the
deviation occurred. For Lakeshore, "you" is the establishment itself, acting through its
Quality function — not your QA personally, not whichever technician first flagged the
reference-table error, and not you as an individual Director. Your QA prepares the filing and
your Quality unit owns the submission, the same way the establishment, not any one employee,
holds the AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) accreditation and
answers to an FDA inspection.

That matters for one more reason: the regulation also closes an obvious loophole. If
Lakeshore ever arranged for someone else to perform a step — a contract testing lab running a
confirmatory assay, a courier handling distribution — while the product was still under
Lakeshore's control, that step counts as performed *under Lakeshore's control*. Lakeshore
can't hand off a processing or distribution step to a contractor and then claim the
contractor, not Lakeshore, owed FDA the report. The reporting duty follows control of the
product, not whoever happened to touch it last.

**How you report has exactly one answer: Form FDA-3486.** Not a memo, not an internal
deviation record forwarded as-is, not an email summary. One specific, named form.

**Where you report also has exactly one answer: CBER**, FDA's Center for Biologics
Evaluation and Research — the one FDA center with authority over blood and blood-component
reporting, not FDA generally and not whichever office handled the routine inspection in
module 1. The regulation gives two acceptable channels for getting the completed form there:
paper, mailed to CBER's own Document Control Center, with the envelope itself marked to
identify that a BPDR is enclosed; or electronic, submitted through CBER's own web-based
filing application. Nothing else qualifies as "filed."

**How this sits next to the recall and next to Lakeshore's own investigation duty.** Two
things are true about the plasma-labeling event at once, and neither one substitutes for the
other. First: the recall already underway (module 2) is about the product itself — getting
the mislabeled units corrected or removed from the hospital's inventory. The BPDR is a
completely separate duty — telling CBER about the deviation that caused the problem. A firm
can file a perfect recall notification and still owe FDA a BPDR it never sent, and vice
versa. Second: 606.171 doesn't just govern reporting outward. It says plainly that Lakeshore's
duty to investigate a biological product deviation internally exists whether or not that
deviation ever had to be reported to FDA at all. Reportability to CBER and the duty to
investigate under Lakeshore's own quality system are two different questions with two
different answers — a deviation can fail the reportability test and still demand a full
internal investigation under Lakeshore's own procedures.

**A one-line reference, not a re-derivation, for the test and the clock already fully taught
in `deviations-and-nonconformances`:** 606.171(b)'s two-prong reportability test (a deviation
that may affect safety, purity, or potency, involving distributed product) and 606.171(c)'s
45-calendar-day reporting clock are settled ground, applied here, not re-walked. The
plasma-labeling event clears (b) without a close call — it's a reference-table deviation that
put the wrong clotting-factor information in a clinician's hands, on a lot that left
Fairview's control and reached a hospital — and the clock on (c) started the day Lakeshore's
label reconciliation caught it, which is where this module's own timeline picks up.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.171(a) | "Six-oh-six point one-seven-one, paragraph a" | **Regulation.** Names who must report — the establishment with control over the product when the deviation occurred — and that a step performed by a contracted party, while the product is under that establishment's control, is still performed "under your control." | Lakeshore's Quality function, not any one individual, owns this filing; the clause closes off outsourcing the reporting duty itself. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(d) | "Paragraph d" | **Regulation.** The report must be made on Form FDA-3486 — no other document satisfies this. | What BPD-0512's filing actually has to be submitted on. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(e), (e)(1), (e)(2) | "Paragraph e, sub-one, sub-two" | **Regulation.** Where the completed form goes — CBER, in paper (to CBER's Document Control Center, envelope marked "BPDR enclosed") or electronic format (CBER's own web-based application). | The two filing channels Lakeshore's QA is choosing between right now. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(f) | "Paragraph f" | **Regulation.** This section supplements, not supersedes, other FDA regulations; *all* biological product deviations — reportable or not — should still be investigated under Parts 211, 606, and 820. | Why Lakeshore's internal investigation duty exists independent of whether BPD-0512 ever had to go to CBER. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(b) / (c) | "Paragraph b / paragraph c" | **Regulation.** The reportability test and the 45-day reporting clock. **Already fully taught in `deviations-and-nonconformances`** — referenced here, not re-quoted. | Confirms BPD-0512 is reportable and that the clock started at discovery; the determination itself isn't redone here. |

## The actual text

21 CFR 606.171(a) — who must report, quoted in full:

> *Who must report under this section?* You, a licensed manufacturer of blood and blood
> components, including Source Plasma; an unlicensed registered blood establishment; or a
> transfusion service who had control over the product when the deviation occurred, must
> report under this section. If you arrange for another person to perform a manufacturing,
> holding, or distribution step, while the product is in your control, that step is performed
> under your control. You must establish, maintain, and follow a procedure for receiving
> information from that person on all deviations, complaints, and adverse events concerning
> the affected product.

Read that middle sentence as the closed loophole it is. Lakeshore never gets to treat a
contracted step as someone else's reporting problem, as long as the product was under
Lakeshore's control when the deviation happened. And the last sentence adds a standing duty
most firms don't think about until they need it: Lakeshore has to have a working procedure
for *receiving* deviation information back from anyone it contracts a step to, not just a
procedure for its own staff.

21 CFR 606.171(d) — how, quoted in full:

> *How do I report under this section?* You must report on Form FDA-3486.

One sentence, one form, no substitutes.

21 CFR 606.171(e), with (e)(1) and (e)(2) — where, quoted in full:

> *Where do I report under this section?* You must send the completed Form FDA 3486 to the
> Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER), either in paper or electronic format.
>
> (1) If you make a paper filing, send the completed form to the CBER Document Control Center
> (see mailing address in § 600.2(a) of this chapter), and identify on the envelope that a
> BPDR (biological product deviation report) is enclosed; or
>
> (2) If you make an electronic filing, send the completed Form FDA3486 electronically using
> CBER's electronic Web-based application.

Two channels, both acceptable, both landing at the same office. 606.171 names the mailing
address only by cross-reference, to § 600.2(a) — a separate section this course doesn't
independently source or quote here, since the operational point is which office, not the
literal street address.

21 CFR 606.171(f) — how this section relates to other FDA regulations, quoted in full:

> *How does this regulation affect other FDA regulations?* This part supplements and does not
> supersede other provisions of the regulations in this chapter. All biological product
> deviations, whether or not they are required to be reported under this section, should be
> investigated in accordance with the applicable provisions of parts 211, 606, and 820 of
> this chapter.

Read that first sentence carefully: "whether or not they are required to be reported." FDA
wrote the reportability test into (b) precisely so that not every deviation has to go to
CBER. (f) then closes the gap that sentence could otherwise leave open: a deviation that
genuinely fails (b)'s test still isn't nobody's problem. It still gets investigated under
Lakeshore's own Part 606 quality system — and under Parts 211 and 820 where they apply.
Reportability to FDA and the duty to investigate internally are two separate questions, and
this is the clause that says so directly, not an inference.

## Filing BPD-0512: the walkthrough

Lakeshore's QA gives this event a tracking label, BPD-0512, distinct from any ID this
curriculum has used before — a new, previously untracked event, not a reuse of `csv-and-
becs`'s DEV-1147 or any other locked finding. Here's what actually goes into filing it,
mapped to 606.171's own lettered structure.

**Who.** The submission is made by Lakeshore's establishment, through its Quality function.
Your QA drafts and assembles the filing; Quality signs and submits it. Fairview's own
technical staff aren't the "who" here any more than the phlebotomist who drew a unit is the
"who" on a donor-eligibility report — the establishment reports, acting through the people its
quality system designates to do so.

**What.** The filing describes the deviation itself: the BECS reference-table error that
caused one code to print PF24 instead of FFP, when the discrepancy was caught (during routine
label reconciliation), what product and how much of it is affected (the one lot, and the
specific units that reached the hospital), and the corrective steps already underway — the
same recall notification already moving under 7.46(a) from module 2, plus whatever
reference-table correction and verification Fairview's team is running now. None of this
requires inventing Form FDA-3486's literal field layout; it requires the same five pieces any
deviation record needs — discovery, containment, extent, disposition, and now the
reportability call applied — organized the way 606.171 asks for.

**How.** Form FDA-3486, per (d). No other document satisfies this regulation, no matter how
thorough Lakeshore's own internal deviation write-up already is.

**Where.** CBER, per (e). The practical choice between paper and electronic is real, and it's
worth a straight recommendation rather than pretending both are equally good defaults.
Electronic filing, through CBER's own web-based application, is the better fit for a modern
blood establishment like Lakeshore running this day to day: it's faster to submit, it
produces a cleaner, time-stamped submission record than a mailed envelope does, and it
removes the mail-transit uncertainty that sits between "we sent it" and "CBER has it" — a
real gap when a 45-day clock is running. Paper still has a place honestly worth naming: a
genuinely down electronic system, a firm with limited access to the web-based application, or
simply an established internal habit some establishments haven't yet moved off of. Neither
channel is more or less compliant than the other — 606.171(e) treats them as equals — but for
an establishment the size of Lakeshore, with BECS infrastructure already in place, electronic
is the practical default and paper is the fallback, not the other way around.

**When.** Discovery was prompt — caught during routine label reconciliation, well before any
unit was issued to a patient — and the filing is going out under a week later. That's
comfortably inside 606.171(c)'s 45-calendar-day clock, with no need to push the filing out to
the deadline just because the deadline exists.

## What CBER's own review would actually look for

CBER isn't reading BPD-0512 to see whether Lakeshore felt bad about it. It's reading for
whether the filing actually answers 606.171's own questions: who's reporting and did they
have control over the product, what the deviation was and what product it touched, that it
landed on Form FDA-3486 rather than some internal substitute, and that it arrived inside the
45-day window with a discovery date that holds up. A filing that's vague about the discovery
date, or that describes the deviation in general terms instead of naming the specific lot and
the specific reference-table error, reads the same way a weak 483 response does: like a firm
that hasn't actually worked through its own facts yet.

## Common traps

**"We already filed the recall paperwork — that covers the BPDR too."** No. 7.46(a)'s
nine-item recall submission (module 2) and Form FDA-3486 ask overlapping but not identical
questions, and they go to different purposes even when they land at the same federal agency.
The recall paperwork is about correcting or removing the product. The BPDR, under 606.171, is
about reporting the deviation that caused the problem. Both draw on the same underlying
facts — what happened, what product is affected — but filing one doesn't file the other, and
Lakeshore owes both for the same event.

**"We determined this isn't reportable, so there's nothing left to do."** Even when that
determination is correct, 606.171(f) says plainly that the investigation duty doesn't
disappear with it. A deviation that genuinely fails (b)'s test still has to be investigated
under Lakeshore's own Part 606 quality system. "Not reportable to CBER" and "not our problem"
are not the same sentence, and (f) exists specifically to make sure nobody reads them as the
same sentence.

## What this means for your job

- **Treat "it's reportable" and "it's filed" as two separate milestones**, with two separate
  completion dates in your own tracking — not one checkbox that closes when the reportability
  call gets made.
- **Ask your QA which channel she used and why**, not just whether the filing went out.
  Electronic, for the reasons above, should be the default answer for a routine filing;
  paper should come with a stated reason, not an unexamined habit.
- **Run the recall and the BPDR as two parallel workstreams, not a sequence.** Neither one
  waits on the other to finish. The recall's pace is driven by how urgently the product needs
  to come off the shelf; the BPDR's pace is driven by its own 45-day clock. Don't let a
  Director's instinct to "finish one thing before starting the next" slow either one down.
- **When a deviation comes back "not reportable," ask what the internal investigation looks
  like anyway** — 606.171(f) means that question doesn't close itself just because CBER never
  sees the file.
- **Know, before an inspector or CBER ever asks, which office a filing went to and how.** "We
  filed BPD-0512 electronically with CBER on [date], inside the 45-day window" is the kind of
  sentence that should come out of your QA without a pause.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says, "If a deviation turns out not to meet 606.171(b)'s reportability test, there's nothing left for us to do with it." Right or wrong?

Wrong, and 606.171(f) is written specifically to correct this. A deviation that genuinely
fails (b)'s test still "should be investigated in accordance with the applicable provisions
of parts 211, 606, and 820" — Lakeshore's own internal investigation duty under its quality
system doesn't depend on whether CBER ever sees a BPDR about it. Reportability to FDA and the
duty to investigate internally are two different questions. A non-reportable deviation with
no internal investigation behind it is still an open gap, even though nothing was ever owed
to CBER.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Is filing BPD-0512 electronically, rather than on paper, a regulatory requirement?

No — and this is worth being precise about. 606.171(e) treats paper and electronic filing as
two equally acceptable channels; nothing in the regulation prefers one over the other.
Recommending electronic filing for an establishment like Lakeshore is this lesson's own
operational judgment — faster, a cleaner time-stamped record, no mail-transit uncertainty
against a 45-day clock — not a requirement the text itself imposes. A paper filing to CBER's
Document Control Center, properly marked "BPDR enclosed," satisfies 606.171 exactly as well.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Lakeshore's recall notification for the plasma lot has already gone out under 7.46(a). Does that satisfy 606.171's reporting duty too?

No. The recall submission and the BPDR are separate obligations that can both apply to the
same event, and one doesn't substitute for the other. 7.46(a)'s nine-item submission is about
correcting or removing the mislabeled product itself. Form FDA-3486, filed under 606.171(d)
and (e), is a distinct report to CBER about the deviation that caused the problem. Both draw
on overlapping facts — what happened, what product is affected — but they're prepared and
filed separately, and BPD-0512 still needs its own BPDR regardless of how the recall
paperwork is going.
:::

## Where this goes next

BPD-0512 is filed: electronically, to CBER, well inside the 45-day window, running in
parallel with the recall already underway and independent of Lakeshore's own internal
investigation into the reference-table error itself. FDA now has what 606.171 requires it to
have. `the-aabb-assessment-process` turns to a completely different reviewer next — one
Lakeshore invites rather than one the law sends, checking Lakeshore's policies, processes, and
procedures against AABB's own Standards rather than against federal regulation, and expecting
things an FDA investigator never asks about.
